name: Kira Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'll try to keep it organised, I tend to answer in lists.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing computer science with a lot of maths, so Monday and Tuesday are algorithms and calculus, Wednesday is the lab, and Thursday I only have a tutorial. I live with my dad Jürgen in a two-room flat near the tram line, about forty minutes from campus. Three afternoons I work the desk at the campus library, and on Saturdays I tutor two school kids in maths. Jürgen lost his factory job last spring and now does temp shifts at a warehouse, so we're careful with everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected, useful in places and overhyped in others. In the library my supervisor Helga says the new catalogue assistant helps with some questions, but people still want a person to ask. I'd keep my opinion to myself online, because I'd rather check facts first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the main thing is still my dad's job. The factory shut because the owners moved production abroad, not because of AI, and the warehouse shifts are never guaranteed. If a plateau means the economy stays flat, his hours stay patchy and I'm the second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the library desk and the tutoring, and I'd ask the library about more hours in the summer. I'd keep a spreadsheet of what we spend, which I already do, and try to build one month of buffer by next spring. And I'd keep using the AI model for explaining proofs I'm stuck on, then check the answer against my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay-ish. Not panicking, but my shoulders are always up near my ears about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the second income. How does that work in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I give my dad two hundred a month towards rent from the library and tutoring. He wouldn't ask, but I know what the bill is. It means I can't just drop a shift if I'm tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if both your income and his dip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we cut the phone plan and the tram pass first, and I'd walk part of the way. I've already planned it on the spreadsheet, row seven. I hate that I know the order, but it helps me sleep.

say: I'd say it's about what I expected, useful in places and **overhyped** in others.
I'd keep my opinion offline until I've checked the **facts**.
think: The main worry is still my dad's patchy **warehouse** shifts, not AI.
If the economy stays flat, I remain the household's **second income**.
do: Keep the library desk and tutoring, and ask for more **summer hours**.
Build one month of buffer by next **spring**.
Keep using AI to explain proofs, then check against my notes.
feel: **Okay-ish**, with shoulders always up near my ears about money.
S0.quote: I give my dad two hundred a month towards rent from the library and tutoring.
fieldNote: Her anxiety comes from **household money** after her father's factory closure, not from AI.
Plans cuts in advance on a **spreadsheet**, a coping habit she admits helps her sleep.
Careful AI use: asks, then verifies against her own notes.

steps.text: Keep the library desk and Saturday tutoring going
Build one month of rent as a buffer by spring
Follow the spreadsheet's order of cuts if income dips
Check AI explanations of proofs against my lecture notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one to take seriously. Writing, checking and coding are what I'm studying, so I'd want to know how entry jobs change. In the library, Helga would say the cataloguing work is shrinking, and I'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think there will still be work for people who can check what the tools produce and explain it. My maths is strong, which helps. But I also think firms will hire fewer juniors and ask them to do more, and I'd be competing with every other top student for fewer spots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course and use the AI tools more regularly, since they're becoming normal. I'd ask lecturers which modules lean towards verification and safety, like formal methods, and I'd pick those. And I'd apply for a summer internship in first year if possible, to get a foot in the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but able to handle it. I'm not the type to be panicked, but I do the maths on money more often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned formal methods. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the part where you prove software does what it should. If machines write the code, someone has to check it, and a person with a strong maths base might be hard to replace. It's a guess, but a reasoned one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your dad's warehouse in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking jobs go first, so the warehouse is safer for now. But the scheduling and ordering get automated, which means fewer supervisors and fewer temp slots. He's an older worker, so any cut would hit him first.

say: I'd say this is the one to **take seriously**, since writing, checking and coding are my field.
I'd agree with Helga that **cataloguing** work is shrinking.
think: People who can check and **explain** what tools produce will still find work.
Firms will hire fewer **juniors**, and I'd compete with every top student for fewer spots.
do: Use AI tools more **regularly**, since they're becoming normal.
Choose modules on **verification** and formal methods.
Apply for a first-year summer internship.
feel: **Tense** but able to cope, and I do the money maths more often.
S1.quote: If machines write the code, someone has to check it, and a person with a strong maths base might be hard to replace.
fieldNote: Her answer is **verification**: using her maths strength to become the person who checks machine-written code.
Notes her father is an older worker and the first to be hit by **supervisor** cuts.
Measured tone; admits the plan is a guess.

steps.text: Use an AI coding assistant weekly in labs and note its errors
Choose formal methods and verification modules
Apply for a summer internship after first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I'd want proper oversight and a pause for safety checks. I'd say it plainly to anyone who'd listen, and I'd write to my representative. But I'd keep my voice low at work, because there I'm the youngest person on the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my dad is in real trouble, and I might be too. He'd be in the middle of his fifties when the robots for hands-on work come in 2031, and I'd be a fresh graduate with a loan. There'd be nothing left to hold either of us up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare hour into paid work, to build a cushion. I'd talk to my mum Anja, who lives in another town, about whether we could pool resources. I'd keep the degree going since it gives access to the university's support, and I'd learn how to use the AI tools to run a small tutoring business online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It would feel like standing in a flat with the water rising and I'm doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pooling with your mum. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has a small flat and a part-time job at a dental office. If my dad and I couldn't pay rent, we'd have to move in with her, and I'd transfer to a university nearby. It wouldn't be great, but it's a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad we need a plan, not a panic. I'd ask him to apply for every training scheme going, and I'd go with him to the first meeting. He's proud and he'd say no, so I'd frame it as me wanting company.

say: I'd say it's too **fast** and I'd want oversight and a pause for safety checks.
I'd write to my representative, while staying quiet at work.
think: My dad is in **real trouble**, and I might be too.
With a loan and no junior jobs, nothing would hold either of us **up**.
do: Put every spare hour into paid work to build a **cushion**.
Talk to my mum Anja about **pooling** resources.
Set up an online maths tutoring business using AI tools.
feel: **Alarmed**, like standing in a flat with the water rising while doing sums.
S2.quote: I'd tell my dad we need a plan, not a panic.
fieldNote: Her fear is **shared**: her father's age and her own debt in the same two years.
Fallback plan with her **mother** is concrete: move in, transfer universities.
Handles her proud father by framing support as company.

steps.text: Ask my mum Anja whether we could move in with her
Start an online maths tutoring business using AI tools
Add extra library and tutoring hours to build a cushion
Go with my dad to a training scheme meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to act sensibly, and I'd want to see what companies and the government actually do. I'd tell friends to read the evidence, not the headlines. I'd keep working and not talk myself into panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd graduate in 2029 and have a short window before robots for hands-on work arrive in 2034. If I get an internship and a good first role, I'd be in a decent position. My dad would be sixty-ish, close enough to retirement that his pension matters more than any retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try for an internship in my second summer, and I'd get comfortable with verification and testing work. I'd look at the pension rules for my dad and see whether a part-time arrangement is possible. And I'd save two hundred a month from the library and tutoring, since I'd rather save than spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious and steady. Five years gives me enough time to prepare, but not so much that I stop watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad's pension come into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He worked twenty-six years at the factory, so he has a partial pension but it isn't large. I'd want to know whether he can claim early and what he'd lose. I'd sit down with him and read the paperwork, because he avoids it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your own debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about the loan, and it only starts to be repaid when I earn above a threshold. I'd use that to my advantage by taking a role where the pay is steady rather than risky. A boring job with a pension suits me better than a gamble.

say: I'd say five years is enough to act **sensibly** and I'd watch what governments do.
I'd tell friends to read the **evidence**, not the headlines.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with a short **window** before hands-on robots arrive in 2034.
My dad would be near retirement, so his **pension** matters more than retraining.
do: Go for a second-summer **internship** and focus on testing work.
Check the **pension** rules and early-claim options with my dad.
Save two hundred a month from library and tutoring wages.
feel: **Cautious** and steady, with enough time to prepare.
S3.quote: A boring job with a pension suits me better than a gamble.
fieldNote: Five years makes her **practical**: pension paperwork with her dad and a steady job over a risky one.
Her stakes include her father's retirement as well as her own career.
Preference is for **security**: she'd choose boring and reliable.

steps.text: Apply for a second-summer internship in software testing
Sit with my dad and read his pension paperwork
Save two hundred a month from library and tutoring
Take the software testing module in second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance to get it right, so let's use it to build safety nets. I'd say it at home and at the library without making a speech. I'd also be the person who reminds friends to keep up their skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can do a proper degree, try two internships and maybe a master's. My dad could retire before the heavy changes arrive, which is a relief. The risk is that ten years lulls everyone, and in year nine there's a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a placement, and put a share of my pay into a pension early, which I'd like to do more than most students. I'd learn the AI tools gradually, like I already do. And I'd spend a bit of time each year reading about where the field is heading, so I'm not surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. Not carefree, but I could manage this. It feels like a long list of things to do rather than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your dad could retire first. How much does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. It would take the biggest worry off my list, and I could stop sending him my wages. I'd feel a bit selfish for caring, but I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for you in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady job in a team that checks software, a small flat, and my dad not having to work. If I had a pension started by then, I'd be happy.

say: I'd say ten years is a chance to get it right and build **safety nets**.
I'd keep reminding friends to keep their skills **current**.
think: I can do a proper degree, two **internships** and maybe a master's.
My dad could retire before the heavy changes arrive, which would be a **relief**.
do: Finish the degree, take a **placement** and start a pension early.
Learn AI tools gradually, as I already do.
Read about where the field is heading each year.
feel: **Steady**; it feels like a long list of tasks, not a threat.
S4.quote: A steady job in a team that checks software, a small flat, and my dad not having to work.
fieldNote: Ten years moves her from household crisis to a **list of tasks**, with her dad's retirement as the key relief.
Warns herself about **complacency**: a rush in year nine.
Wants security: pension, steady team, small flat.

steps.text: Start paying into a pension during my placement year
Use an AI tool weekly and read about the field each year
Apply for a master's in software verification
Help my dad plan his retirement date

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my dad and I would be hit in the same two years and there'd be no cushion. What would help is early warning from the government, help for older workers like him to retrain or retire, and a loan system that doesn't start charging me before I have a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I think it's that people assume a computer science student must be fine. I'm fine on paper, with good grades. At home it's a spreadsheet and a tram pass, and I'd like people to know that.

headlineQuote: At home it's a spreadsheet and a tram pass, and I'd like people to know that.
portrait: **Kira** is an eighteen-year-old computer science and maths student who works at the campus library and tutors on Saturdays.
She lives with her dad, who lost his factory job, and gives him part of her wages for **rent**.
Careful and organised, she uses AI tools now and then, verifies them, and plans cuts in advance on a **spreadsheet**.
Her mood runs anxious through most scenarios because her **household** and her debt are exposed together.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because her father and she would be hit in the same two years with no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Early **warning** from government, retraining or retirement help for older workers, and a loan that doesn't charge before a job.
